title: Day 1 · Phase 1 — Re-anchoring: what if it hits, and could we nudge it?
bodyHtml:
DAY 1 · Phase 1 — Setting up the question

Unit 2 told us WHERE 2026-XJ is going. Unit 3 asks: what happens if Earth is in the way — and is there anything we could do about it?

TODAY'S LEARNING TARGETS (preview)

K1. Momentum as a measure of "motion that's hard to stop." R3. Why deflecting an asteroid is a momentum problem (preview).

K = Knowledge; R = Reasoning; S = Skill. Use the unit target list for the full wording.

THE ASTEROID THREAD TODAY

What students know about 2026-XJ as today opens: Students have considered how gravity bends the fictional asteroid’s path. This unit asks what an impact or a deliberate momentum transfer could change, using the scenario data supplied in class.

How today connects:

end of Unit 2, students computed closest approach. The closest approach number is uncomfortably close.

Today's pivot: Two questions Unit 3 will answer. (1) If 2026-XJ collides with Earth, what's the physics that decides what happens? (2) NASA actually deflected an asteroid in 2022 (DART mission). What did they do, and would it work for our asteroid?

Lesson Flow

(Assumes a ~50-minute period; adjust for block schedule.)

TimeWhat happens
0–5 min

• Return Unit 2 transfer tasks. Highlight any group that got the asteroid closest-approach reasonable. "You know where it's going. Now: what if Earth is in the way?"

5–18 min

• Demo: roll a small Hot Wheels car gently into a cardboard wall — nothing happens. Roll the same car FAST — wall buckles. Then take a HEAVIER cart at the slow speed — wall buckles. Ask: "What MAKES a moving thing hard to stop?"

18–28 min

• Notice & Wonder. Lead the class to name TWO things that matter: how MUCH stuff is moving (mass) and how FAST it's moving (velocity). Tease: "There's a single number that combines both. We call it momentum."

28–42 min

• Mini-lecture preview: Unit 3 has two big payoffs. One: what 2026-XJ's IMPACT looks like in physics terms (Days 12–13). Two: the 2022 DART mission, where NASA bumped an asteroid by a few cm/s and changed its orbit. Show a 30-second DART animation if available.

42–48 min

• Individual exit: Two carts move in the same direction at +2 m/s. Cart A has mass 1 kg; cart B has mass 3 kg. Both are brought to rest in 1 s. Which requires the larger change in momentum and average stopping force? Explain using the controlled comparison. Then predict what changes if cart A starts at +4 m/s instead. Name one question this raises about deflecting an asteroid.

48–50 min

• Marzano on K1/R3 preview.

FORMATIVE CHECKS (how teacher knows what students are getting)

Compare predictions before and after the controlled cart trials. Look for explicit control of stopping time when students compare average stopping force.

Next teaching move: Sort the individual responses by the named misconception above. Begin the next meeting with a short diagram or comparison for students who need it; use a new example to check whether the reasoning changed.

MATERIALS & READING

Materials and setup: Unit 2 transfer tasks scored; Hot Wheels car + a heavier cart (or block + tape); cardboard or thin foam target; clear floor zone; DART mission animation bookmarked.

Hewitt reading: CPA: no reading. Honors: Ch 8 §8.1.

Honors companion reading — OpenStax College Physics for AP® Courses 2e: Alongside the Honors Hewitt assignment above, read §8.1 Linear Momentum and Force (pp. 344–346). Focus: Introduce momentum as a vector and compare how mass and velocity affect an impact or a proposed nudge. Page numbers are printed book pages; read only the named section or excerpt on shared pages.

TEACHER NOTES

• Individual exit: Two carts move in the same direction at +2 m/s. Cart A has mass 1 kg; cart B has mass 3 kg. Both are brought to rest in 1 s. Which requires the larger change in momentum and average stopping force? Explain using the controlled comparison. Then predict what changes if cart A starts at +4 m/s instead. Name one question this raises about deflecting an asteroid.

Differentiation: ELs — sentence frame "_____ would be harder because _____"; SWDs — verbal version of exit ticket offered; Honors extension — "if we made a number 'mass times velocity,' what would the units be?"

Online sequence: observe the controlled trials before opening the mass-and-speed explanation. Avoid comparing injury from a car and bullet as a momentum assessment; stopping time, contact area and material would confound it.

CPA teaching sequence: Draw before-and-after arrows and choose a positive direction. Supply components for two-dimensional examples, use a mass–velocity–momentum table, model one calculation step at a time, then fade the table for the individual response.

Language and access: Offer the same physics prompt and rubric with a labeled visual, word bank, optional sentence starter, and oral rehearsal. A student may explain through supported writing, a labeled sketch, or an oral response when appropriate to the task; retain the reasoning demand. In an assessment, use only the previously agreed access supports, without giving a worked solution.

Collect the individual evidence before the 1–3 target self-rating. Use the evidence to choose the next teaching step; completion, video viewing, and a student self-rating do not set a teacher mastery rating.

title: Day 2 · Phase 2 — Momentum p = mv
bodyHtml:
DAY 2 · Phase 2 — Building the tools

p = mv. Units kg·m/s. Vector — direction matters.

TODAY'S LEARNING TARGETS

K1. Momentum definition + vector nature. S1. Compute momentum.

K = Knowledge; R = Reasoning; S = Skill. Use the unit target list for the full wording.

THE ASTEROID THREAD TODAY

What students know about 2026-XJ as today opens: Students have considered how gravity bends the fictional asteroid’s path. This unit asks what an impact or a deliberate momentum transfer could change, using the scenario data supplied in class. The preceding meeting focused on Re-anchoring: what if it hits, and could we nudge it?.

How today connects:

What's 2026-XJ's momentum? Big number. Numbing big. Today we build the scale of "big-momentum object" vs. "small-momentum object" so the asteroid math lands later.

Lesson Flow

(Assumes a ~50-minute period; adjust for block schedule.)

TimeWhat happens
0–5 min

• Hand back Day 1 exit tickets. Lift any student wording that's close to "combine mass and speed." Anchor: today's the day we define it.

5–15 min

• Direct instruction: p = mv. Units: kg·m/s. Vector — same direction as velocity. Write it big on the board.

15–30 min

• Worked example sequence: (1) 1500-kg car at 30 m/s east. (2) 0.05-kg bullet at 400 m/s east. (3) 70-kg sprinter at 10 m/s east. (4) 5×10⁶-kg cruise ship at 8 m/s east. (5) 2026-XJ at its current speed — pick a sensible asteroid mass + velocity. Put the five momenta side-by-side. Magnitudes wildly different.

30–42 min

• Quick practice — packet has 6 problems mixing mass + velocity, including a couple where direction matters (vector signs).

42–48 min

• Exit ticket: "A 0.15-kg baseball moving at 40 m/s east meets the bat. After it bounces back at 50 m/s WEST, what is the CHANGE in its momentum?" (Vector subtraction; force the sign.)

48–50 min

• Marzano on K1/S1.

FORMATIVE CHECKS (how teacher knows what students are getting)

Check signed velocities and momentum units kg·m/s. In a reversal, students must subtract signed momenta rather than subtract speed magnitudes.

Next teaching move: Sort the individual responses by the named misconception above. Begin the next meeting with a short diagram or comparison for students who need it; use a new example to check whether the reasoning changed.

MATERIALS & READING

Materials and setup: packet problems printed; calculator availability; the five-example momentum table pre-drawn on the board.

Hewitt reading: CPA: Ch 8 §8.1. Honors: Ch 8 §8.1 + Think and Solve 54.

Honors companion reading — OpenStax College Physics for AP® Courses 2e: Alongside the Honors Hewitt assignment above, revisit §8.1 Linear Momentum and Force (pp. 344–346). Focus: Calculate signed momentum and distinguish momentum from force and speed. Page numbers are printed book pages; read only the named section or excerpt on shared pages.

TEACHER NOTES

Talk moves on the baseball exit ticket: students will subtract the magnitudes. Push: "What direction is positive? What direction is the final velocity? What's the actual sign of v_f?"

Differentiation: ELs — provide a units-only example (kg × m/s = kg·m/s); SWDs — pre-printed table for the 5 worked examples; Honors extension — "compute momentum of Earth (6×10²⁴ kg) moving at 30 km/s around the Sun."

CPA teaching sequence: Draw before-and-after arrows and choose a positive direction. Supply components for two-dimensional examples, use a mass–velocity–momentum table, model one calculation step at a time, then fade the table for the individual response.

Language and access: Offer the same physics prompt and rubric with a labeled visual, word bank, optional sentence starter, and oral rehearsal. A student may explain through supported writing, a labeled sketch, or an oral response when appropriate to the task; retain the reasoning demand. In an assessment, use only the previously agreed access supports, without giving a worked solution.

Collect the individual evidence before the 1–3 target self-rating. Use the evidence to choose the next teaching step; completion, video viewing, and a student self-rating do not set a teacher mastery rating.

title: Day 3 · Phase 2 — Impulse + impulse-momentum theorem
bodyHtml:
DAY 3 · Phase 2 — Building the tools

J = FΔt = Δp. The bridge between force (Unit 1) and momentum (Unit 3).

TODAY'S LEARNING TARGETS

K2. Impulse-momentum theorem. S2. Compute impulse and Δp.

K = Knowledge; R = Reasoning; S = Skill. Use the unit target list for the full wording.

THE ASTEROID THREAD TODAY

What students know about 2026-XJ as today opens: Students have considered how gravity bends the fictional asteroid’s path. This unit asks what an impact or a deliberate momentum transfer could change, using the scenario data supplied in class. The preceding meeting focused on Momentum p = mv.

How today connects:

To CHANGE 2026-XJ's momentum we need to apply a force OVER A TIME. The DART mission did exactly that — a small force, applied briefly, changed asteroid momentum by a tiny but measurable amount. Today's math IS the DART math.

Lesson Flow

(Assumes a ~50-minute period; adjust for block schedule.)

TimeWhat happens
0–5 min

• Quick check: write p = mv. Units? Vector or scalar?

5–18 min

• Derivation move: start from F = ma = m·Δv/Δt. Multiply both sides by Δt: FΔt = mΔv = Δp. Name FΔt as impulse (J). Units: N·s = kg·m/s (same as momentum).

18–30 min

• Worked example: 0.15-kg baseball changes from +40 m/s to -50 m/s. Δp = ? If the bat-ball contact lasts 0.002 s, what FORCE did the bat apply?

30–42 min

• Group practice — 5 problems mixing knowns: sometimes you know F and Δt, find Δp. Sometimes you know Δp and Δt, find F.

42–48 min

• Exit ticket: "DART hit its asteroid for 0.05 s with an average force of 8×10⁵ N. What change in asteroid momentum did it deliver?"

48–50 min

• Marzano on K2/S2. Tomorrow: WHY does impulse matter beyond the math?

FORMATIVE CHECKS (how teacher knows what students are getting)

Look for impulse as change in momentum, with N·s equivalent to kg·m/s. Check the direction of the change as well as its magnitude.

Next teaching move: Sort the individual responses by the named misconception above. Begin the next meeting with a short diagram or comparison for students who need it; use a new example to check whether the reasoning changed.

MATERIALS & READING

Materials and setup: packet practice problems; calculator availability; the J = FΔt = Δp triangle on the board.

Hewitt reading: CPA: Ch 8 §8.2. Honors: Ch 8 §8.2–8.3 + Think and Solve 56, 60, 61.

Honors companion reading — OpenStax College Physics for AP® Courses 2e: Alongside the Honors Hewitt assignment above, read §8.2 Impulse (pp. 347–350). Focus: Connect impulse to change in momentum and the force-time graph; identify average force and interaction time. Page numbers are printed book pages; read only the named section or excerpt on shared pages.

TEACHER NOTES

Talk moves on the derivation: watch for students who don't see WHY FΔt equals Δp. Stop. "Where in F = ma is there a time? Where is there a velocity change?" Have them point.

Differentiation: ELs — vocab card (impulse / impulso, momentum / cantidad de movimiento); SWDs — pre-printed Δp = p_f − p_i column for each problem; Honors extension — "impulse equals area under an F-vs-t graph. Why?" (Calculus preview.)

CPA teaching sequence: Draw before-and-after arrows and choose a positive direction. Supply components for two-dimensional examples, use a mass–velocity–momentum table, model one calculation step at a time, then fade the table for the individual response.

Language and access: Offer the same physics prompt and rubric with a labeled visual, word bank, optional sentence starter, and oral rehearsal. A student may explain through supported writing, a labeled sketch, or an oral response when appropriate to the task; retain the reasoning demand. In an assessment, use only the previously agreed access supports, without giving a worked solution.

Collect the individual evidence before the 1–3 target self-rating. Use the evidence to choose the next teaching step; completion, video viewing, and a student self-rating do not set a teacher mastery rating.

title: Day 4 · Phase 2 — Why impulse matters: airbags, follow-through, padding
bodyHtml:
DAY 4 · Phase 2 — Building the tools

To get the SAME Δp you can use BIG force / SHORT time, or SMALL force / LONG time. That choice is everywhere.

TODAY'S LEARNING TARGETS

R1. Reason about how varying Δt (or F) achieves a given Δp.

K = Knowledge; R = Reasoning; S = Skill. Use the unit target list for the full wording.

THE ASTEROID THREAD TODAY

What students know about 2026-XJ as today opens: Students have considered how gravity bends the fictional asteroid’s path. This unit asks what an impact or a deliberate momentum transfer could change, using the scenario data supplied in class. The preceding meeting focused on Impulse + impulse-momentum theorem.

How today connects:

To deflect 2026-XJ we want the LARGEST Δp possible. So we want the longest contact time AND/OR the biggest force. DART did short-and-hard. Other concepts (gravity tractor, ion engine push) do long-and-soft.

Lesson Flow

(Assumes a ~50-minute period; adjust for block schedule.)

TimeWhat happens
0–5 min

• Hook: drop an egg onto concrete (don't actually — show video). Then drop one into a pillow. Same Δp. Different F. Why?

5–18 min

• Direct instruction: J = FΔt. For a fixed Δp, FΔt is FIXED. Bigger Δt → smaller F. Bigger Δt → safer. Airbags. Crumple zones. Follow-through in baseball/tennis (extends contact). Padded floors in gyms.

18–32 min

• Group case study analysis — pairs pick one of: airbag, helmet, boxing glove, gymnastics mat, car crumple zone, parkour roll. Articulate the SAME Δp / longer Δt / smaller F logic for their scenario.

32–42 min

• Worked example: 80-kg sprinter going 9 m/s stops in 0.05 s (concrete) vs. 0.5 s (foam pit). Compute F for each. Show the 10× difference.

42–48 min

• Exit ticket: "A boxer 'rolls with the punch.' Why does this hurt LESS for the same Δp?"

48–50 min

• Marzano on R1.

FORMATIVE CHECKS (how teacher knows what students are getting)

Hold the momentum change fixed while comparing stopping times. A longer stopping time reduces average force; it does not erase the required impulse.

Next teaching move: Sort the individual responses by the named misconception above. Begin the next meeting with a short diagram or comparison for students who need it; use a new example to check whether the reasoning changed.

MATERIALS & READING

Materials and setup: short video clips (egg + pillow, car crash test with vs. without airbag); case study cards printed; calculator availability.

Hewitt reading: CPA: Ch 8 §8.3. Honors: Ch 8 §8.3 + Think and Solve 60, 62.

Honors companion reading — OpenStax College Physics for AP® Courses 2e: Alongside the Honors Hewitt assignment above, revisit §8.2 Impulse (pp. 347–350). Focus: Explain how a longer stopping time changes average force for the same momentum change. Page numbers are printed book pages; read only the named section or excerpt on shared pages.

TEACHER NOTES

Talk moves on "safer" reasoning: students may say "bigger Δt means less momentum." Stop. "Did the momentum CHANGE? Or did the FORCE delivering the change change?"

Differentiation: ELs — visual pairs (no padding/padded) with arrows showing Δt; SWDs — pre-built table for the case study with two columns (situation / impulse logic); Honors extension — "design an asteroid deflection that uses long Δt instead of short. What would it look like?"

CPA teaching sequence: Draw before-and-after arrows and choose a positive direction. Supply components for two-dimensional examples, use a mass–velocity–momentum table, model one calculation step at a time, then fade the table for the individual response.

Language and access: Offer the same physics prompt and rubric with a labeled visual, word bank, optional sentence starter, and oral rehearsal. A student may explain through supported writing, a labeled sketch, or an oral response when appropriate to the task; retain the reasoning demand. In an assessment, use only the previously agreed access supports, without giving a worked solution.

Collect the individual evidence before the 1–3 target self-rating. Use the evidence to choose the next teaching step; completion, video viewing, and a student self-rating do not set a teacher mastery rating.

title: Day 5 · Phase 2 — Conservation of momentum: explosions + recoil
bodyHtml:
DAY 5 · Phase 2 — Building the tools

Σp_before = Σp_after. No external force means momentum's conserved.

TODAY'S LEARNING TARGETS

K3. State conservation of momentum + its condition (no net external force).

K = Knowledge; R = Reasoning; S = Skill. Use the unit target list for the full wording.

THE ASTEROID THREAD TODAY

What students know about 2026-XJ as today opens: Students have considered how gravity bends the fictional asteroid’s path. This unit asks what an impact or a deliberate momentum transfer could change, using the scenario data supplied in class. The preceding meeting focused on Why impulse matters: airbags, follow-through, padding.

How today connects:

When DART hit its target, total momentum BEFORE = total momentum AFTER. The asteroid sped up because the spacecraft slowed down (and got destroyed). Same logic, asteroid-scale.

Lesson Flow

(Assumes a ~50-minute period; adjust for block schedule.)

TimeWhat happens
0–3 min

• Quick recap: J = Δp. What gives a Δp? External force × time.

3–15 min

• The flip: if NO external force acts on a SYSTEM, total p of the system doesn't change. Demo: two carts (different masses) at rest with a compressed spring between, released. They recoil. Σp_before = 0. Σp_after = m₁v₁ + m₂v₂ = 0. The smaller cart moves faster.

15–28 min

• Worked example: 70-kg ice skater throws a 5-kg ball at 8 m/s east. Skater recoils west at what speed? Show the algebra.

28–40 min

• Group practice — 4 explosion/recoil problems. Mix masses + velocities. Include a rocket-style problem (continuous case treated as before/after).

40–48 min

• Exit ticket: "A 0.5-kg firework explodes at rest into two pieces: a 0.3-kg piece moving east at 12 m/s, and a 0.2-kg piece moving — what direction and how fast?"

48–50 min

• Marzano on K3.

FORMATIVE CHECKS (how teacher knows what students are getting)

Check that students define a system containing both interacting objects and state the negligible-external-impulse condition before using conservation.

Next teaching move: Sort the individual responses by the named misconception above. Begin the next meeting with a short diagram or comparison for students who need it; use a new example to check whether the reasoning changed.

MATERIALS & READING

Materials and setup: two carts + spring (or two skateboards + students if no carts); practice problems printed; calculator availability.

Hewitt reading: CPA: Ch 8 §8.4. Honors: Ch 8 §8.4 + Think and Solve 51, 64.

Honors companion reading — OpenStax College Physics for AP® Courses 2e: Alongside the Honors Hewitt assignment above, read §8.3 Conservation of Momentum (pp. 350–354). Focus: Choose the interacting system and check external impulse before applying momentum conservation to recoil or separation. Page numbers are printed book pages; read only the named section or excerpt on shared pages.

TEACHER NOTES

Talk moves on the cart demo: after the carts recoil, ask: "What was the total momentum BEFORE? What's the total momentum AFTER? How do those numbers compare? Why?" Push them to articulate the rule.

Differentiation: ELs — diagram with arrows for each object's velocity, before/after; SWDs — fill-in-the-blank conservation equation with placeholders; Honors extension — "a rocket continuously expels exhaust. How does conservation of momentum explain thrust?"

CPA teaching sequence: Draw before-and-after arrows and choose a positive direction. Supply components for two-dimensional examples, use a mass–velocity–momentum table, model one calculation step at a time, then fade the table for the individual response.

Language and access: Offer the same physics prompt and rubric with a labeled visual, word bank, optional sentence starter, and oral rehearsal. A student may explain through supported writing, a labeled sketch, or an oral response when appropriate to the task; retain the reasoning demand. In an assessment, use only the previously agreed access supports, without giving a worked solution.

Collect the individual evidence before the 1–3 target self-rating. Use the evidence to choose the next teaching step; completion, video viewing, and a student self-rating do not set a teacher mastery rating.

title: Day 6 · Phase 2 — Collisions: elastic, inelastic, perfectly inelastic
bodyHtml:
DAY 6 · Phase 2 — Building the tools

Momentum's always conserved. Energy's only conserved in elastic ones. Stick-together = perfectly inelastic.

TODAY'S LEARNING TARGETS

K4. Distinguish elastic, inelastic, perfectly inelastic collisions.

K = Knowledge; R = Reasoning; S = Skill. Use the unit target list for the full wording.

THE ASTEROID THREAD TODAY

What students know about 2026-XJ as today opens: Students have considered how gravity bends the fictional asteroid’s path. This unit asks what an impact or a deliberate momentum transfer could change, using the scenario data supplied in class. The preceding meeting focused on Conservation of momentum: explosions + recoil.

How today connects:

An asteroid striking Earth would be PERFECTLY INELASTIC — the asteroid effectively becomes part of Earth (after vaporizing). A glancing flyby with no contact would be ELASTIC (gravity scattering only). DART was somewhere in between — momentum delivered, but the spacecraft was destroyed.

Lesson Flow

(Assumes a ~50-minute period; adjust for block schedule.)

TimeWhat happens
0–5 min

• Quick check: conservation of momentum rule + condition.

5–18 min

• Three categories on the board: Elastic (bounce, no KE loss), Inelastic (bounce, some KE lost), Perfectly inelastic (stick together, max KE lost). All three: momentum IS conserved.

18–32 min

• Demos: superball off concrete = nearly elastic. Clay ball off concrete = inelastic. Velcro carts colliding and sticking = perfectly inelastic. After each, ask: "Where did the energy go in this case?"

32–42 min

• Vocabulary practice: classify 8 real-world collisions (car crash, billiard balls, football tackle, baseball + bat, asteroid impact, two magnets repelling without contact, etc.). Pair-share.

42–48 min

• Exit ticket: "A meteorite buries itself in the desert. What kind of collision is this? Where did its kinetic energy go?"

48–50 min

• Marzano on K4. Tomorrow: Vernier collision lab.

FORMATIVE CHECKS (how teacher knows what students are getting)

Listen for the distinction between conserved system momentum and kinetic energy. Sticking together identifies a perfectly inelastic collision; it does not make momentum disappear.

Next teaching move: Sort the individual responses by the named misconception above. Begin the next meeting with a short diagram or comparison for students who need it; use a new example to check whether the reasoning changed.

MATERIALS & READING

Materials and setup: superball, clay ball, Velcro carts (or carts + masking tape), concrete or hard tile surface, classification worksheet.

Hewitt reading: CPA: Ch 8 §8.5. Honors: Ch 8 §8.5 + Think and Solve 57, 58, 65.

Honors companion reading — OpenStax College Physics for AP® Courses 2e: Alongside the Honors Hewitt assignment above, read §8.4 Elastic Collisions in One Dimension (pp. 354–356); §8.5 Inelastic Collisions in One Dimension (pp. 356–360). Focus: Distinguish elastic, inelastic, and perfectly inelastic collisions. Momentum conservation and kinetic-energy conservation are different claims. Page numbers are printed book pages; read only the named section or excerpt on shared pages.

TEACHER NOTES

Talk moves on the demo: after the clay ball, ask: "Why DIDN'T the clay bounce? What changed?" Push toward energy lost to deformation/heat.

Differentiation: ELs — three-column visual (elastic / inelastic / perfectly inelastic) with one example each; SWDs — fewer classification items, more partner discussion; Honors extension — "is any real collision PERFECTLY elastic? When is the approximation good?"

CPA teaching sequence: Draw before-and-after arrows and choose a positive direction. Supply components for two-dimensional examples, use a mass–velocity–momentum table, model one calculation step at a time, then fade the table for the individual response.

Language and access: Offer the same physics prompt and rubric with a labeled visual, word bank, optional sentence starter, and oral rehearsal. A student may explain through supported writing, a labeled sketch, or an oral response when appropriate to the task; retain the reasoning demand. In an assessment, use only the previously agreed access supports, without giving a worked solution.

Collect the individual evidence before the 1–3 target self-rating. Use the evidence to choose the next teaching step; completion, video viewing, and a student self-rating do not set a teacher mastery rating.

title: Day 7 · Phase 2 — Vernier collision lab: verify conservation
bodyHtml:
DAY 7 · Phase 2 — Building the tools

Two Vernier carts. Two photogates. Run elastic and inelastic collisions. Compare Σp_before to Σp_after.

TODAY'S LEARNING TARGETS

S4. Vernier collision measurement. K3. Conservation of momentum, experimental confirmation.

K = Knowledge; R = Reasoning; S = Skill. Use the unit target list for the full wording.

THE ASTEROID THREAD TODAY

What students know about 2026-XJ as today opens: Students have considered how gravity bends the fictional asteroid’s path. This unit asks what an impact or a deliberate momentum transfer could change, using the scenario data supplied in class. The preceding meeting focused on Collisions: elastic, inelastic, perfectly inelastic.

How today connects:

If conservation of momentum holds in our lab carts, we can TRUST it for asteroids too. Today's lab is the empirical foundation for the asteroid math on Days 11–13.

Lesson Flow

(Assumes a ~50-minute period; adjust for block schedule.)

TimeWhat happens
0–5 min

• Lab procedure overview. Safety: tracks level, carts at gentle pushes only, photogates clamped.

5–18 min

• Teacher demo: one elastic collision (magnet-bumpered carts) — read v_before and v_after off photogates. Compute Σp_before and Σp_after. Show they match.

18–38 min

• Lab: pairs run 2 trials of an elastic collision (magnets) and 2 of a perfectly inelastic collision (Velcro). Record v_before and v_after for each cart. Compute Σp_before and Σp_after. Compare.

38–42 min

• Class data compilation: % difference between Σp_before and Σp_after across all groups. Discuss sources of error (friction on track, photogate timing, mass measurement).

42–45 min

Individual exit: Explain one result from today using a labeled sketch, calculation, or specific observation. State the model or relationship you used and one assumption. Use your own evidence before comparing with a partner.

45–48 min

• Lab write-up start (data + claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph). Homework finish.

48–50 min

• Marzano on S4.

FORMATIVE CHECKS (how teacher knows what students are getting)

Inspect measured masses and signed before-and-after velocities. Compare system momentum with uncertainty and possible external impulse from the track.

Next teaching move: Sort the individual responses by the named misconception above. Begin the next meeting with a short diagram or comparison for students who need it; use a new example to check whether the reasoning changed.

MATERIALS & READING

Materials and setup: Vernier dynamics carts + tracks + magnet bumpers + Velcro pads; photogates + LabQuest interfaces; balance for cart masses; lab write-up template.

Hewitt reading: CPA: no reading. Honors: no reading.

Honors companion reading — OpenStax College Physics for AP® Courses 2e: Alongside the Honors Hewitt assignment above, revisit §8.3 Conservation of Momentum (pp. 350–354); §1.3 Accuracy, Precision, and Significant Figures (pp. 27–29). Focus: Plan how to compare total momentum before and after the collision while accounting for measurement uncertainty. Page numbers are printed book pages; read only the named section or excerpt on shared pages.

TEACHER NOTES

Talk moves on the % difference: if a group is at 8% off, push: "What in the setup leaked momentum out of your system? Was the track tilted? Did the cart drag?"

Differentiation: ELs — partner with a LoggerPro-fluent student; SWDs — pre-assigned roles (driver / scribe / equation-checker); Honors extension — "the elastic collision lost SOME momentum on paper. Where? Estimate the missing % from track friction."

CPA teaching sequence: Draw before-and-after arrows and choose a positive direction. Supply components for two-dimensional examples, use a mass–velocity–momentum table, model one calculation step at a time, then fade the table for the individual response.

Language and access: Offer the same physics prompt and rubric with a labeled visual, word bank, optional sentence starter, and oral rehearsal. A student may explain through supported writing, a labeled sketch, or an oral response when appropriate to the task; retain the reasoning demand. In an assessment, use only the previously agreed access supports, without giving a worked solution.

Collect the individual evidence before the 1–3 target self-rating. Use the evidence to choose the next teaching step; completion, video viewing, and a student self-rating do not set a teacher mastery rating.

title: Day 8 · Phase 2 — Inelastic collision math: stick-together problems
bodyHtml:
DAY 8 · Phase 2 — Building the tools

m₁v₁ + m₂v₂ = (m₁ + m₂) v_f. The clean case.

TODAY'S LEARNING TARGETS

S3. Solve perfectly inelastic 1D collision problems.

K = Knowledge; R = Reasoning; S = Skill. Use the unit target list for the full wording.

THE ASTEROID THREAD TODAY

What students know about 2026-XJ as today opens: Students have considered how gravity bends the fictional asteroid’s path. This unit asks what an impact or a deliberate momentum transfer could change, using the scenario data supplied in class. The preceding meeting focused on Vernier collision lab: verify conservation.

How today connects:

An asteroid impact is the planetary version of "stick together and continue." Today's math is exactly the framework we'd use to estimate Earth-system velocity change from a 2026-XJ impact.

Lesson Flow

(Assumes a ~50-minute period; adjust for block schedule.)

TimeWhat happens
0–5 min

• Quick recap of yesterday's lab. Did the inelastic trials confirm conservation? Within how much %?

5–15 min

• Set up the inelastic equation: m₁v₁ + m₂v₂ = (m₁ + m₂) v_f. Walk through it as a special case of total conservation.

15–28 min

• Worked example 1: classic ballistic pendulum — 0.05-kg bullet at 400 m/s into a 5-kg block at rest. Find v_f of bullet-plus-block.

28–40 min

• Worked example 2: two cars colliding head-on and locking together (one east, one west). Find final velocity. Force direction reasoning.

40–46 min

• Quick practice — 3 problems on a worksheet.

46–48 min

• Exit ticket: "A 1000-kg car at 20 m/s east rear-ends a 2000-kg stalled truck. They lock. What's the final velocity?"

48–50 min

• Marzano on S3.

FORMATIVE CHECKS (how teacher knows what students are getting)

Check a shared final velocity for the joined objects, total final mass, and signs for head-on motion. Ask whether the result lies between the initial velocities.

title: Day 9 · Phase 2 — Elastic collision math: bounce-apart problems
bodyHtml:
DAY 9 · Phase 2 — Building the tools

Both momentum AND kinetic energy conserved. Two equations, two unknowns.

TODAY'S LEARNING TARGETS

S3. Solve 1D elastic collision problems.

K = Knowledge; R = Reasoning; S = Skill. Use the unit target list for the full wording.

THE ASTEROID THREAD TODAY

What students know about 2026-XJ as today opens: Students have considered how gravity bends the fictional asteroid’s path. This unit asks what an impact or a deliberate momentum transfer could change, using the scenario data supplied in class. The preceding meeting focused on Inelastic collision math: stick-together problems.

How today connects:

A flyby with no contact is essentially elastic — gravity scatters the asteroid, momentum and energy both conserved. The math here is what we'd use to predict an asteroid's path AFTER a gravity-assist swing-by.

Lesson Flow

(Assumes a ~50-minute period; adjust for block schedule.)

TimeWhat happens
0–5 min

• Quick recap: elastic = both p and KE conserved.

5–18 min

• Set up: two equations. Σp: m₁v₁ᵢ + m₂v₂ᵢ = m₁v₁f + m₂v₂f. ΣKE: ½m₁v₁ᵢ² + ½m₂v₂ᵢ² = ½m₁v₁f² + ½m₂v₂f². Two unknowns (v₁f, v₂f). Solvable.

18–32 min

• Worked example: 0.5-kg ball at 4 m/s strikes a 1.0-kg ball at rest elastically. Find both final velocities. (Use the simplified result for one-at-rest: v₁f = ((m₁−m₂)/(m₁+m₂))v₁ᵢ; v₂f = (2m₁/(m₁+m₂))v₁ᵢ.)

32–42 min

• Pattern-finding: what happens when m₁ = m₂? When m₁ ≫ m₂? When m₁ ≪ m₂? Use the simplified formulas to predict, then check with PhET Collision Lab.

42–48 min

• Exit ticket: "A 0.2-kg superball at 5 m/s east strikes a 0.2-kg ball at rest, elastically. What happens to each?"

48–50 min

• Marzano on S3.

FORMATIVE CHECKS (how teacher knows what students are getting)

Check both system momentum and kinetic energy for an ideal elastic model. Equal masses exchange velocities in the one-dimensional special case; that rule does not cover every collision.

Next teaching move: Sort the individual responses by the named misconception above. Begin the next meeting with a short diagram or comparison for students who need it; use a new example to check whether the reasoning changed.

MATERIALS & READING

Materials and setup: PhET Collision Lab on lab computers; simplified-formula reference card; calculator.

Hewitt reading: CPA: no reading. Honors: Ch 8 §8.5 + Think and Solve 59.

Honors companion reading — OpenStax College Physics for AP® Courses 2e: Alongside the Honors Hewitt assignment above, revisit §8.4 Elastic Collisions in One Dimension (pp. 354–356). Focus: Use the one-dimensional elastic-collision model and check both momentum and the speed-dependent energy condition. Page numbers are printed book pages; read only the named section or excerpt on shared pages.

TEACHER NOTES

Talk moves on the equal-mass case: after the formulas predict v₁f=0, v₂f=v₁ᵢ, push: "Newton's cradle. What just happened? Does that match the result?"

Differentiation: ELs — formula card with each symbol labeled; SWDs — students can use the simplified formulas without re-deriving; Honors extension — "derive the simplified one-at-rest formulas from the two conservation equations."

CPA teaching sequence: Draw before-and-after arrows and choose a positive direction. Supply components for two-dimensional examples, use a mass–velocity–momentum table, model one calculation step at a time, then fade the table for the individual response.

Language and access: Offer the same physics prompt and rubric with a labeled visual, word bank, optional sentence starter, and oral rehearsal. title: Day 10 · Phase 2 — 2D collisions: glancing blows
bodyHtml:
DAY 10 · Phase 2 — Building the tools

Conservation applies COMPONENT-WISE: Σpₓ before = Σpₓ after. Same for y.

TODAY'S LEARNING TARGETS

R2. Apply 2D conservation of momentum to glancing collisions.

K = Knowledge; R = Reasoning; S = Skill. Use the unit target list for the full wording.

THE ASTEROID THREAD TODAY

What students know about 2026-XJ as today opens: Students have considered how gravity bends the fictional asteroid’s path. This unit asks what an impact or a deliberate momentum transfer could change, using the scenario data supplied in class. The preceding meeting focused on Elastic collision math: bounce-apart problems.

How today connects:

An asteroid that's NUDGED doesn't move in a straight line afterward — it deflects sideways. 2D momentum is the framework for asking "how much sideways?" Critical for DART-style deflection analysis tomorrow.

Lesson Flow

(Assumes a ~50-minute period; adjust for block schedule.)

TimeWhat happens
0–5 min

• Hook: billiard balls. A cue ball strikes a stationary ball at an angle. Both move off in different directions. Both p_x and p_y must balance.

5–18 min

• Direct instruction: vector momentum p has p_x and p_y components. Conservation applies SEPARATELY to each: Σpₓ_before = Σpₓ_after; Σpᵧ_before = Σpᵧ_after. Two equations.

18–32 min

• Worked example: 0.16-kg cue ball at 2 m/s east strikes a 0.16-kg stationary ball. After: cue ball goes 1 m/s at 30° north of east. What's the second ball's velocity (magnitude + direction)?

32–42 min

• Practice — 3 problems on PhET Collision Lab in 2D mode. Vary angles. Predict, then check.

42–48 min

• Exit ticket: "Why must p_x AND p_y each be conserved separately, not just total p?"

48–50 min

• Marzano on R2.

FORMATIVE CHECKS (how teacher knows what students are getting)

Check separate x and y momentum accounts, with labeled directions. Provide components for CPA; Honors students can derive them and justify the angles.

Next teaching move: Sort the individual responses by the named misconception above. Begin the next meeting with a short diagram or comparison for students who need it; use a new example to check whether the reasoning changed.

Materials and setup: PhET Collision Lab with 2D mode enabled; billiards image; vector decomposition reference from Unit 1.

Focus: Apply momentum conservation separately in perpendicular directions; use components for glancing collisions. Page numbers are printed book pages; read only the named section or excerpt on shared pages.

TEACHER NOTES

title: Day 11 · Phase 2 — DART mission case study: nudging an asteroid
bodyHtml:
DAY 11 · Phase 2 — Building the tools

NASA's DART crashed into Dimorphos in 2022 and changed its orbital period by 32 minutes.

TODAY'S LEARNING TARGETS

R3. Reason about asteroid deflection using momentum + impulse.

K = Knowledge; R = Reasoning; S = Skill. Use the unit target list for the full wording.

THE ASTEROID THREAD TODAY

What students know about 2026-XJ as today opens: Students have considered how gravity bends the fictional asteroid’s path. This unit asks what an impact or a deliberate momentum transfer could change, using the scenario data supplied in class. The preceding meeting focused on 2D collisions: glancing blows.

How today connects:

This is the day we ask: COULD we deflect 2026-XJ? If DART changed Dimorphos's orbit measurably, what would it take to do the same to our asteroid? The unit's been building to this question.

Lesson Flow

(Assumes a ~50-minute period; adjust for block schedule.)

TimeWhat happens
0–5 min

• Brief: who knows about DART? Show a 1-minute mission animation.

5–18 min

• Case study direct instruction: DART was ~600 kg, hit Dimorphos (~5×10⁹ kg) at ~6 km/s. Use conservation of momentum (perfectly inelastic) to estimate the velocity change Δv given to the asteroid.

18–32 min

• Compute Δv. (Will be a few mm/s.) Discuss: that's TINY. Why does it matter? Because it accumulates over years — the asteroid's POSITION drifts further off course every orbit.

32–41 min

• Group problem: 2026-XJ has a mass of (give a value, maybe 10⁹ kg) and a closest-approach trajectory bringing it within (say 50,000 km of Earth). What Δv would deflect it by an Earth-radius offset, given (say 6 months) lead time? Run the numbers.

41–44 min

Individual exit: Explain one result from today using a labeled sketch, calculation, or specific observation. State the model or relationship you used and one assumption. Use your own evidence before comparing with a partner.

44–48 min

• Discussion: is the required Δv DART-scale or much bigger? What does this tell us about real planetary defense?

48–50 min

• Marzano on R3.

FORMATIVE CHECKS (how teacher knows what students are getting)

Look for momentum transfer and a small change in velocity accumulating a displacement over time. Students must state the simple model's assumptions before scaling it to a real orbit.

Next teaching move: Sort the individual responses by the named misconception above. Begin the next meeting with a short diagram or comparison for students who need it; use a new example to check whether the reasoning changed.

MATERIALS & READING

Materials and setup: DART mission animation bookmarked; case study card with DART numbers; calculator availability; whiteboard space.

Hewitt reading: CPA: no reading. Honors: Ch 8 §8.4 + Think and Solve 64.

Honors companion reading — OpenStax College Physics for AP® Courses 2e: Alongside the Honors Hewitt assignment above, revisit §8.2 Impulse (pp. 347–350); §8.3 Conservation of Momentum (pp. 350–354). Focus: Use impulse and system momentum as the model for the DART case. Mission measurements and ejecta details come from the assigned case-study sources. Page numbers are printed book pages; read only the named section or excerpt on shared pages.

TEACHER NOTES

Talk moves on the tiny Δv: when students balk at "3 mm/s," push: "Multiply that by how many seconds are in a year. How many kilometers off course does that put it?"

Differentiation: ELs — provide the DART numbers with units pre-labeled; SWDs — pre-built calculation worksheet with steps; Honors extension — "what if DART had been twice as fast? Would Δv be twice or four times bigger?" (Linear in speed.)

CPA teaching sequence: Draw before-and-after arrows and choose a positive direction. Supply components for two-dimensional examples, use a mass–velocity–momentum table, model one calculation step at a time, then fade the table for the individual response.

title: Day 12 · Phase 2 — Asteroid impact: what momentum says about damage
bodyHtml:
DAY 12 · Phase 2 — Building the tools

If deflection fails, what does the impact look like in physics terms?

TODAY'S LEARNING TARGETS

R2/R3. Apply momentum and impulse to estimate impact effects (preview to Unit 4 energy).

K = Knowledge; R = Reasoning; S = Skill. Use the unit target list for the full wording.

THE ASTEROID THREAD TODAY

What students know about 2026-XJ as today opens: Students have considered how gravity bends the fictional asteroid’s path. This unit asks what an impact or a deliberate momentum transfer could change, using the scenario data supplied in class. The preceding meeting focused on DART mission case study: nudging an asteroid.

How today connects:

If 2026-XJ hits Earth, momentum is the FIRST framework we'd use. Earth's velocity changes by (almost nothing — because Earth's mass is colossally larger). But the asteroid's momentum is delivered to a small impact zone over a short time — that's the impulse that does the damage.

Lesson Flow

(Assumes a ~50-minute period; adjust for block schedule.)

TimeWhat happens
0–5 min

• Frame: "Today we play out the other branch. Deflection fails. It hits."

5–15 min

• Use Unit 2's velocity prediction + a reasonable 2026-XJ mass. Compute the asteroid's momentum at impact.

15–30 min

• Apply impulse-momentum theorem to the impact: contact time ≈ 0.1 s (asteroid stops). What's the AVERAGE force? Convert to a meaningful unit (compare to a building, an earthquake).

30–42 min

• Class discussion: what does this LARGE force not capture? (Energy. Heat. Shockwave.) Tease Unit 4: kinetic energy at impact gives a more useful damage estimate. Today's number is one PART of the picture.

42–48 min

• Exit ticket: "Why is Earth's velocity change after an asteroid impact essentially zero, even though the impact is catastrophic locally?"

48–50 min

• Marzano.

FORMATIVE CHECKS (how teacher knows what students are getting)

Check that average force depends on the assumed collision duration. Momentum alone does not determine crater size or damage; students should identify the need for energy and material information.

Next teaching move: Sort the individual responses by the named misconception above. Begin the next meeting with a short diagram or comparison for students who need it; use a new example to check whether the reasoning changed.

MATERIALS & READING

Materials and setup: 2026-XJ parameter card (mass, impact velocity from Unit 2); calculator; reference for "how big is a Newton" (1 N ≈ apple weight).

Hewitt reading: CPA: no reading. Honors: Ch 8 §8.2 + Think and Solve 55, 56.

Honors companion reading — OpenStax College Physics for AP® Courses 2e: Alongside the Honors Hewitt assignment above, revisit §8.2 Impulse (pp. 347–350). Focus: Distinguish momentum change from average force; stopping time and interaction details are needed before making a damage claim. Page numbers are printed book pages; read only the named section or excerpt on shared pages.

TEACHER NOTES

Talk moves on Earth's negligible Δv: push: "Earth's mass is 10²⁴ kg. The asteroid's mass is 10⁹ kg. Look at the ratio. Now look at the velocity Earth gains."

Differentiation: ELs — equation laid out with each term labeled; SWDs — provide the numbers on a step-card; Honors extension — "if the impact angle is 30° from vertical, how does that change the momentum delivered HORIZONTALLY?"

CPA teaching sequence: Draw before-and-after arrows and choose a positive direction. Supply components for two-dimensional examples, use a mass–velocity–momentum table, model one calculation step at a time, then fade the table for the individual response.

Language and access: Offer the same physics prompt and rubric with a labeled visual, word bank, optional sentence starter, and oral rehearsal. A student may explain through supported writing, a labeled sketch, or an oral response when appropriate to the task; retain the reasoning demand. Lesson Flow

(Assumes a ~50-minute period; adjust for block schedule.)

TimeWhat happens
0–5 min

Retrieve yesterday’s work and plan. Identify what must be completed before the defense.

5–25 min

Work independently to complete the analysis and public-facing explanation. Teacher help remains limited to task clarification and agreed access supports.

25–40 min

Peer defense: Each student explains the model, evidence, and limits while the partner uses the four-dimension rubric to ask questions and leave a specific feedback note. Switch roles. Explain your own work; do not copy or replace it with a partner’s solution.

40–48 min

Make a short final revision based on the questions raised. Mark what changed and why. Complete a separate 0–4 self-rating for each rubric dimension and a brief reflection.

48–50 min

Submit the task, planning sheet, peer feedback, revisions, and four-dimension self-rating. Identify one next step for feedback. The following meeting begins the next unit.

TRANSFER TASK

• Transfer task. Independent. 4 multi-part problems: (1) compute momentum + impulse for a baseball-bat collision; (2) perfectly inelastic collision with measured shared final velocity (use momentum; do not require a pendulum-height energy method); (3) 2D billiards collision with both balls' final velocities; (4) asteroid deflection — given a Δv from a DART-style impact, how much lead time produces a 6400-km lateral shift?

Public-facing transfer: Write a public-facing explanation of how a momentum change and lead time affect a possible deflection of 2026-XJ. State the limits of the simplified model.

FORMATIVE CHECKS (how teacher knows what students are getting)

Listen for explanations that cite the student’s own work and the four rubric dimensions. Check whether a revision answers a specific question, whether uncertainty is acknowledged, and whether the student can defend the model without a partner supplying it.

Compare the self-rating with the evidence when giving feedback. Record the teacher’s judgments independently; peer agreement or completion is not a mastery score.

Work retained from the first meeting; the same task and permitted references; calculators; four-dimension rubric; peer-feedback sheet; final reflection and submission folder.

Hewitt reading: CPA: no new reading. Honors: no new reading during assessment.

Honors companion reading — OpenStax College Physics for AP® Courses 2e: No new OpenStax reading during the transfer assessment. Use only the references permitted in the assessment plan; revisit a focused section after feedback.

TEACHER NOTES

Assessment conventions: Use the Unit 1 rubric: Science / Reasoning / Communication / Transfer-to-Asteroid. Score the four dimensions independently from 0–4; report the profile without averaging and use the established lowest-dimension conversion. Science checks the physics; Reasoning checks the choice and justification of the model; Communication checks labeled, organized work; Transfer-to-Asteroid checks the supported connection and its limits. Peer and student ratings are feedback; the teacher makes the final judgment. Target self-ratings use the separate 1–3 scale and do not automatically become mastery ratings. Revisions follow Unit 1’s two-week window, with new evidence for a one-level move on a dimension.

Offer the same physics prompt and rubric with a labeled visual, word bank, optional sentence starter, and oral rehearsal. A student may explain through supported writing, a labeled sketch, or an oral response when appropriate to the task; retain the reasoning demand. In an assessment, use only the previously agreed access supports, without giving a worked solution.
